title: Contribute

Metadata consistency checklist
Before opening a pull request:

identifiers are stable and not session-specific
marker names match existing identifiers in mapfile.tsv
group_id and marker_group_id use lowercase identifiers without spaces
taxonomy is consistent from Kingdom to Species
missing taxonomy ranks are coded as NA
added files are not cluster-specific
input/ncbi.creds and other private credentials are never committed

title: Workflow
text: VirMarkDB documents how the database is generated, how marker-specific HMM profiles are built and applied, and how the database is refined through assessment-guided detection of missing or underrepresented diversity. The same pipeline is applied uniformly across the three viral groups currently covered — giant viruses, phages, and RNA viruses — each genome being searched only against the marker-group profiles relevant to its taxonomic scope.

Each row defines one marker group: a marker gene, a taxonomic scope, a reference protein set, and the HMM profile built from it. title: Workflow
text:
Pipeline

1 · ORF prediction: ORFs are predicted from each genome with Prodigal in metagenomic mode (prodigal -p meta). Script: 02_prodigal.bash
2 · Alignment: Marker-group reference proteins are aligned with MAFFT (mafft --ep 0 --genafpair). Script: 03_align_markers.bash
3 · HMM profile construction: Alignments are converted to HMM profiles with HMMER hmmbuild. Script: 04_hmmbuild.bash
4 · HMM search: Predicted ORF proteomes are searched with hmmsearch against the marker-group profiles assigned via genome_marker_map.tsv. Script: 05_hmmsearch.bash
5 · Hit selection: For each genome × marker-group pair, hits are ranked by increasing e-value then decreasing bit score. The best-ranked hit is always kept; additional hits are kept only if close to the best in both score and length. Script: 06_final_results.R



Filter
Threshold




Score ratio relative to best hit
≥ 0.80


Length ratio relative to best hit
≥ 0.80

title: Database
text:
Why marker groups exist
Some marker genes are too divergent across viral lineages to be represented by a single HMM profile. VirMarkDB solves this with marker groups: each one ties together a marker gene, a taxonomic scope, a reference protein set, and a dedicated HMM profile built from that set. This keeps a common marker-gene framework across the database while letting each lineage be represented by a profile calibrated on its own reference sequences.






Note



This page describes the concept. The mechanics (how mapfile.tsv encodes marker groups and drives the pipeline) are covered once, in Workflow → Marker-group configuration.

title: About
text:
Notes and limitations
ORF prediction. ORFs are predicted with Prodigal in metagenomic mode. This approach is practical and robust, but some viral coding sequences may still be difficult to predict correctly. Introns, inteins, sequencing artefacts, or internal stop codons may lead to truncated or fragmented predicted proteins.
Partial genome records. Some source genomes are partial. Missing markers in those entries may reflect incomplete sequence coverage rather than true biological absence.
HMM profile performance. Profile sensitivity depends on the diversity, quality, and taxonomic coverage of the seed reference protein sets. Under-represented lineages may show lower detection rates.
Marker-group scope. HMM profiles are defined per marker group, each linking a marker gene, a taxonomic scope, a reference protein set, and a corresponding HMM profile. Divergent lineages outside current marker-group scope may not be detected reliably.
Missing value interpretation. NA or zero values in marker presence tables mean not detected or not retained under the current workflow and thresholds, not confirmed biological absence.
External protein assessment. The external protein assessment is an empirical procedure designed to identify potentially missing or underrepresented marker diversity in VirMarkDB. It should not be interpreted as a formal performance benchmark based on a ground-truth dataset.
Current taxonomic scope. The database currently covers three viral groups: giant viruses (Nucleocytoviricota), phages (Pantevenvirales, via g23), and RNA viruses (Orthornavirae, via rdrp). Additional viral groups will be added as suitable marker references and genome mappings become available.

title: VirMarkDB
text:
A curated reference database of viral marker-gene sequences for giant viruses, phages and RNA viruses
VirMarkDB provides protein/nucleotide sequences for ten conserved marker genes across three viral groups: giant viruses (Nucleocytoviricota), phages (Pantevenvirales) and RNA viruses (Orthornavirae), built from ICTV-derived taxonomy.
